name: Basil
label: basil block

planting.note: 4-8 in apart (Johnny's); 16 plants in two 8-ft rows; pinch tips to force branching

bed30.note: three rows across a 30 in bed, 8 in in-row (Johnny's 4-8 in); cut whole plants 4-6 in above ground for a second flush

watch_for: BASIL DOWNY MILDEW — the big one in the Northeast since 2007 (yellowing between veins, grey spores under leaves; wind-borne, doesn't overwinter here, Cornell/UConn); Japanese beetles; fusarium wilt
watering: Regular moisture — basil is not drought tolerant (Johnny's); water the soil, keep leaves dry to slow downy mildew.
method_notes: Warm-season ANNUAL — never out until nights stay above 50°F (Johnny's). Coleman-style: transplant-first at 6 weeks, dense spacing, and pinch the growing tip once plants are 6-8 in for a low, leafy plant. Harvest before flowering by cutting back to a pair of side shoots; strip flower buds to hold the window open. UMaine's Maine Home Garden News puts basil with the tender plants set out in June, and with tomatoes in the same bed is the classic pairing.
source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Genovese 68 d, 4-8 in spacing, sow 6 wk indoors); Cornell vegetables and UConn IPM basil downy mildew factsheets; UMaine Maine Home Garden News June 2025 (tender annuals; basil+tomato).

name: Dill
label: dill row

planting.note: sow two 8-ft rows, 1/4 in deep; thinning barely needed if you harvest leaves young

bed30.note: three rows across a 30 in bed sown thin; Johnny's says thinning is not necessary for leaf harvest

watch_for: BOLTING — dill 'bolts quickly in hot conditions' (Johnny's); sow early and in successions rather than fighting July; parsleyworm (black swallowtail caterpillar — let it eat, it becomes a butterfly); aphids
watering: Even moisture; don't let young plants dry out or they rush to seed.
method_notes: Cool-season ANNUAL; direct-sow as soon as the soil can be worked and again every ~3 weeks (Johnny's) to keep leaf coming. In the bed system it is as much insectary as herb: UMaine (MHGN June 2025) and UNH's insectary-plant research both place flowering dill among the top hoverfly attractants — hoverfly larvae eat aphids — and UMaine notes dill draws tiger swallowtails. Let every third plant flower rather than stripping it, and it pays the bed back.
source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Bouquet 40-45 d to leaf, 85-105 d to seed; succession sowings every 3 wk); Fedco (Bouquet 55 d, 'especially attractive to pollinators'); UMaine MHGN June 2025 (hoverflies, let herbs flower); UNH Extension insectary-plant research report 2017-18.

name: Parsley
label: parsley row

planting.note: 12 plants ~9 in apart; seeds germinate notoriously slowly (14-30 d, Johnny's), so start early

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart; Johnny's thins direct-sown parsley to 8-12 in

watch_for: parsleyworm (black swallowtail caterpillar), Septoria leaf spot in wet spells, and second-year bolting — it is a biennial and wants to flower year two
watering: Moist, fertile soil; clip outer leaves and it keeps producing all season.
method_notes: COOL-season biennial grown as an annual but a real winter survivor: Johnny's notes parsley 'wintered over' in a well-drained spot gives an early spring crop (mulch where it goes below 0°F), and parsley is on Eliot Coleman's list of ~30 cold-hardy crops grown through winter in the unheated greenhouses of the Winter Harvest Handbook. Slow germination is the whole trick — start indoors ~9-10 weeks (Johnny's) or soak patience. Establish by August for winter use.
source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Giant of Italy 75 d; germ 14-30 d; winter-over & mulch notes; 9-10 wk indoor start); Eliot Coleman, The Winter Harvest Handbook (parsley among cold-hardy winter greenhouse crops, ch. 8); extension parsley maturity ~70-90 d.

name: Cilantro
label: cilantro strip

planting.note: two 8-ft rows sown 1/4 in deep; keeps better in cool weather than summer heat

bed30.note: three rows, 4 in in-row; it is a leaf crop, so density is fine

watch_for: BOLTING — cilantro 'bolts quickly in hot conditions' (Johnny's); heat and long days trigger it, so the crop is spring and fall, not July; aphids on new growth
watering: Steady moisture, lighter afternoon shade in heat; drought = instant bolting.
method_notes: Cool-season ANNUAL, the fastest leaf herb in the bed. Direct-sow in successions every 2 weeks and pull whole plants when leaves are full. UNH's insectary research found cilantro among the top hoverfly attractants of the plants tested, so let a few plants flower for the bed even as you strip the rest. If you want coriander seed, stop picking and it will set seed ~90-105 days in.
source: Fedco (Caribe & Leisure 55 d; Longstanding 30 d leaf / 45 d seed, 'grows best in cool temperatures'); Johnny's (bolting note; succession practice); UNH Extension insectary-plant research report 2017-18 (cilantro among top hoverfly attractants).

name: Thyme
label: thyme edge

planting.note: 16 plants at 6-8 in (Johnny's) — small, low, and happy at the bed edge

bed30.note: three rows at 8 in; thyme stays short and spreads, so it also works as the bed's front edging

watch_for: WINTERKILL in wet, poorly drained beds — Johnny's advises cutting only a few stems the first year 'in order for the plants to winter over'; root rot in soggy soil; spider mites in summer drought
watering: Dry, well-drained soil and little water — it sulks in wet feet.
method_notes: MARGINALLY HARDIY perennial in zone 5b — reliable only in the driest, best-drained bed (or gravel); treat the first year gently to get it through winter (Johnny's). Seed is slow (90-95 d, Johnny's) so transplant, and pinch tips for bushiness. Thyme goes woody and needs division or replacement after 3-4 years (Johnny's). UMaine's bee research clocked garden thyme among the most-visited herbs in Maine.
source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (German Winter 90-95 d; 8-10 wk indoor start; light first-year harvest to winter over; woody after 3-4 yr); UMaine Bulletin #2076, Selecting Plants to Support Bees in Maine (garden thyme, high June visitation).

name: Oregano
label: oregano row

planting.note: 8 plants at 12 in (Johnny's); it sprawls, so give it room

bed30.note: two rows at 12 in; cut back after flowering to keep it tidy

watch_for: aphids on new growth; root rot in heavy wet soil — otherwise about the easiest herb in Maine; divide every few years as the center dies out
watering: Likes it dry once established; water only in long drought.
method_notes: RELIABLY HARDIY perennial in zone 5b; Greek oregano is the culinary one. UMaine's four-year bee study (Bulletin #2076) counted oregano among the most-visited, longest-flowering bee plants of everything tested — a flowering oregano plant is doing pollinator duty for the bee-pollinated crops in the beds around it. Slow from seed (Johnny's 8-10 wk indoors); harvest just as flowers begin to open.
source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (oregano 80-90 d; 8-10 wk indoor start); UMaine Bulletin #2076 (oregano among most-visited bee plants, Greek oregano photographed with bumble bee); UMaine MHGN June 2025 (oregano with tomatoes).

name: Sage
label: sage corner

planting.note: 4 plants at 12-18 in (Johnny's 12 in) — it becomes a 16-30 in woody shrub

bed30.note: two rows at 15 in; give it a corner or bed end so it doesn't shade leafy neighbors

watch_for: winterkill in wet heavy soil (sage wants sharp drainage); spider mites in drought; plants go woody and are best replaced every few years (Johnny's)
watering: Very drought-tolerant; water only in extended dry spells.
method_notes: RELIABLY HARDIY perennial in zone 5b (Johnny's lists zones 4-8), but it rots in wet winters, so put it in the sandiest bed corner. Classic companion-planting pairing with carrots and the cabbage family; starts slowly from seed (6-8 wk inside, Johnny's), so buying one plant or taking divisions is the fast route. Cut stems as flowers start to open for the strongest flavor.
source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Common Sage 80-90 d; 6-8 wk indoor start; zones 4-8; spacing 12 in; woody replacement note); classic companion lists (Burpee: sage with cabbage family & carrots); UMaine MHGN June 2025 lists sage among pollinator-friendly herbs.

name: Rosemary
label: rosemary pot

planting.note: 4 plants at 8-10 in when grown as an annual (Johnny's); it wants warmth and sharp drainage

bed30.note: two rows at 12 in; Johnny's: plant 8-10 in apart as an annual, 24-36 in only if it overwinters

watch_for: ROOT ROT from wet feet (its #1 killer in Maine; Johnny's wants well-drained soil); powdery mildew and spider mites when overwintered indoors
watering: Let the soil dry between waterings; never soggy, and keep it warm — it sulks below 50°F.
method_notes: TENDER PERENNIAL in zone 5b — Johnny's lists it zones 6-10, and UMaine's Maine Home Garden News groups rosemary with the tender perennials you grow as annuals here (or overwinter in a pot in a sunny window). Slow from seed (10-12 wk inside, Johnny's); many Maine gardeners just buy a plant. Harvest of stem tips begins ~80-100 days from planting (Johnny's). In the bean bed, old companion lists credit it with deterring bean beetles.
source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (rosemary 10-12 wk indoor start; zones 6-10; 80-100 d to first harvest; 8-10 in as annual spacing); UMaine Maine Home Garden News June 2025 (rosemary among tender perennials grown as annuals, pollinator-friendly); Burpee companion chart (rosemary deters bean beetles).

name: Mint
label: mint tub

planting.note: 4 plants at 12-18 in (Johnny's) — but ONLY in a sunken tub or barrier; see method_notes

bed30.note: two rows, but plan for the runner: a buried pot or edging barrier is mandatory or mint owns the bed in one season

watch_for: MINT RUST (Puccinia menthae — orange pustules under leaves; also infects marjoram and savory, per RHS) — cut out infected shoots before spores blacken; aphids; spider mites in drought
watering: Moist soil is fine, but water the soil in the morning and never overhead — wet leaves invite rust.
method_notes: RELIABLY HARDIY perennial in zone 5b (Johnny's: zones 4-9), and the one herb that must be CONTAINED: Johnny's own culture notes warn it 'may become invasive in the field.' Coleman and Damrosch plant mints in sunken pots or dedicated beds with barriers — planted bare in a 30-in bed it will colonize half the garden by August. Young transplants withstand some freezing (Johnny's) so it goes out early. Rust management is the only real chore: thin stems for airflow, remove spotted shoots, don't compost them.
source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Common mint 70-80 d; zones 4-9; 6-8 wk indoor start; 'may become invasive in field'); RHS mint rust (Puccinia menthae; also infects marjoram & savory); PNW Pest Management Handbooks (Mentha rust); Coleman/Damrosch bed practice (contained planting).

name: French Tarragon
label: tarragon corner

planting.note: 4 divisions at 12-18 in; propagate by spring root divisions or cuttings — NEVER from seed

bed30.note: two rows at 15 in in the driest corner of the bed

watch_for: WINTERKILL — hardy to zone 4 per USU, but crowns rot in wet Maine winters, so plant in the best-drained spot and mulch the crown; aphids; spider mites in drought
watering: Dry and lean — too much water kills it faster than cold does.
method_notes: MARGINALLY HARDIY perennial in zone 5b. The essential fact: TRUE FRENCH TARRAGON IS A STERILE CLONE — it sets no viable seed, so anything grown from seed is Russian tarragon, which is nearly flavorless (USU Extension). Buy a plant, then propagate it by spring root divisions or stem cuttings (USU). The 90-120 day figure is an honest estimate to a full first picking from a spring division — no seed catalog lists a days-to-maturity because none sell true French tarragon seed. Divide every 3-4 years to keep flavor strong.
source: Utah State University Extension, French Tarragon in the Garden (sterile clone; divisions/cuttings only; winter hardy to zone 4; Russian tarragon from seed is flavorless); no catalog DTM exists — 90-120 d estimated from a spring division.

name: Summer savory
label: savory edge

planting.note: 12 plants at 6-8 in; direct-sow or set out after frost

bed30.note: three rows at 8 in; it stays a tidy 12 in and finishes fast

watch_for: mostly pest-free — occasional aphids; if it bolts in a heat wave, cut it back and it resprouts from the base
watering: Even moisture while young; drought-tolerant once growing.
method_notes: COOL-season ANNUAL with real frost tolerance — a late-summer sowing gives a fall crop (UMaine lists summer savory with the sturdy herbs that dry easily; classic companion charts put it at the base of bean plants to deter Mexican bean beetles and improve bean flavor — Burpee's chart spells out both). It is the annual stand-in for winter savory, which is a perennial (Fedco) but stronger and coarser-flavored.
source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Summer Savory 60-70 d); Burpee companion chart (summer savory deters bean beetles, improves growth & flavor of beans; also an onion ally); Fedco (winter savory, Satureja montana, 100 d perennial, 'stronger and more pungent').

name: Bulb fennel
label: fennel row

planting.note: 8 plants at 6 in (Johnny's); plant 'to mature in shortening days' — a Maine fall crop, not a July one

bed30.note: two rows at 8 in; Johnny's: disturb the roots as little as possible or it bolts

watch_for: BOLTING — triggered by heat, long days, and root disturbance at transplant (Johnny's); aphids; parsleyworm; clip any seed stalks that form (Johnny's)
watering: Adequate, steady irrigation — water stress and heat push it straight to seed (Johnny's).
method_notes: COOL-season ANNUAL — Johnny's is blunt: plant fennel 'to mature in shortening days with cooler temperatures, as high heat and long days encourage bolting.' In coastal Maine that means a midspring sowing for bulbs by late summer, or a summer sowing for fall bulbs. Bulbs tolerate light frost, so it is a legitimate September-October crop here. Transplant gently in 4-6 weeks or direct-sow; the bulb is swollen leaf bases, harvested when the base thickens (Johnny's). No strong companion claims — fennel is the herb most companion charts tell you to plant apart.
source: Johnny's Selected Seeds Fino fennel (maturity from direct seeding; cool-season bolting guidance; 6 in spacing; 4-6 wk transplant; clip seed stalks); growingtaste.com & gardeningknowhow variety roundups (Zefa Fino ~65-80 d, short-season favorite); UMaine MHGN June 2025 (fennel among herbs drawing tiger swallowtails when allowed to flower).

name: Sweet marjoram
label: marjoram row

planting.note: 12 plants at 6-8 in (Johnny's); a small soft herb that tolerates crowding

bed30.note: three rows at 8 in; pinch growing tips to force branching (Johnny's)

watch_for: root rot in soggy soil; aphids; wilts fast if the soil dries — Johnny's: it 'will not tolerate dry soils'
watering: Moist, never dry, never soggy — the one Mediterranean herb that wants regular water.
method_notes: TENDER PERENNIAL — Johnny's lists marjoram zones 9-11 and Fedco bluntly says 'grown as an annual in the North': in zone 5b plant it like a summer annual and don't expect it back. UMaine's Maine Home Garden News groups marjoram with the pollinator-friendly plants that 'don't survive our winters.' Start indoors 8-10 weeks (Johnny's); harvest whole plants just as flowering begins. Same genus as oregano but it is the soft, tender, winter-tender cousin.
source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Sweet marjoram 80-95 d; zones 9-11; 8-10 wk indoor start; 6-8 in spacing; drought note); Fedco (Origanum majorana 80-95 d, 'grown as an annual in the North'); UMaine MHGN June 2025 (marjoram among pollinator-friendly tender perennials).

name: Chervil
label: chervil strip

planting.note: two 8-ft rows sown shallow (light needed to germinate, Johnny's); also sow ~60 days before first frost for fall

bed30.note: three rows at 4 in — a tight, low, fast crop that wants cool weather

watch_for: BOLTS fast in heat — Fedco: 'in warmer locations performs best as a fall crop'; slugs in wet springs; keep cut so it doesn't flower
watering: Light but constant moisture (Fedco); it is a cool-weather plant that hates dry spells.
method_notes: COOL-season ANNUAL and the classic French fine herbe, too delicate for drying. Slow-bolting strains (Fedco's) aside, treat it as early-spring and fall crop: Johnny's culture calls for direct sowing in early spring and again ~60 days before first frost. It self-sows if you let it. Chervil is standard in Eliot Coleman's winter-salad greenhouse mix in the Winter Harvest Handbook, and in the summer bed it is happier in the shade of taller crops (classic lettuce-bed partner).
source: Fedco (Chervil 60 d to full maturity; harvest leaves 6-8 wk after sowing; fall-crop note; mesclun staple); Johnny's Selected Seeds (chervil culture: direct sow spring + 60 d before first frost; 6 in spacing; light needed to germinate); Eliot Coleman, The Winter Harvest Handbook (chervil as winter greenhouse salad crop).

name: Calendula
label: calendula edge

planting.note: 12 plants at 6-12 in (Johnny's); direct-sow or start 4-5 wk inside

bed30.note: three rows at 8 in, or use it as the bed's front edge — it flowers from June to hard frost

watch_for: powdery mildew in humid late summer; aphids on buds; NOTE: UNH insectary research found calendula also hosted imported cabbageworm — keep it off the brassica beds if you can
watering: Rich, well-drained soil (Johnny's); steady water, deadhead daily for continuous bloom.
method_notes: COOL-season hardy ANNUAL — frost-tolerant, so it goes out early and flowers 'from summer to heavy frost' (Johnny's, which recommends 2-3 sowings 3 weeks apart for continuous bloom). UMaine's four-year bee study singles out 'pot marigold' as one of three direct-seeded annuals that flower long without deadheading and reseed themselves year after year — plant it once on the bed edge and it runs itself. Also a hoverfly flower in UMaine's June 2025 article; but see the UNH caveat about cabbageworm.
source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Flashback Mix 50-55 d; spacing 6-12 in; 2-3 successive sowings; flowers to heavy frost); UMaine Bulletin #2076 (pot marigold among top self-sowing direct-seeded bee annuals); UMaine MHGN June 2025 (calendula listed as pollinator-friendly annual); UNH insectary research report 2017-18 (calendula hosted imported cabbageworm).

name: Chamomile (German)
label: chamomile strip

planting.note: 12 plants at 8 in (Johnny's); press seeds onto the surface — light needed to germinate

bed30.note: three rows at 8 in; 15-24 in tall, airy, self-sows everywhere

watch_for: aphids in the flower heads; pick flowers at full bloom and keep picking — Johnny's says 3-4 cuttings a season
watering: Sandy, well-drained soil (Johnny's); water steadily while establishing, then let it be.
method_notes: The garden tea chamomile is GERMAN chamomile (Matricaria recutita), a COOL-season hardy ANNUAL — 60-65 days to flower (Johnny's). Johnny's culture notes it 'self-sows readily. May become invasive, if allowed to do so' — in a kitchen-garden bed that is a feature: one planting becomes a permanent volunteer. (Roman chamomile, Chamaemelum nobile, is the hardy-groundcover perennial alternative.) Classic companion charts credit chamomile with improving onions (Burpee). Harvest timing only: gather flowers in full bloom.
source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Common Chamomile, Matricaria recutita, 60-65 d; 8 in spacing; light-needed germination; self-sows readily note; 3-4 cuttings); Burpee companion chart (chamomile improves onion growth and flavor).

name: Borage
label: borage station

planting.note: 4 plants at 12 in (Johnny's) — a taprooted 2-3 ft plant; DIRECT-SOW, transplants hate it (Johnny's)

bed30.note: two rows at 12 in; one or two plants near bee-pollinated crops does the pollinator job

watch_for: aphids cluster on flower stems late summer; powdery mildew if crowded; everything else ignores it
watering: Average soil, little water once up — it 'grows well even in poor soils' (Johnny's).
method_notes: Hardy ANNUAL and the single best bee flower in UMaine's four-year study — common borage was among the most-visited plants of ~90 tested, and UMaine lists it as one of three direct-seeded annuals that reseed themselves year after year (Bulletin #2076). Plant one or two near the squash/cucumber rows for pollination, and let them set seed: they'll come back forever. Johnny's: direct-sow after soil warms, thin to 12 in, harvest flowers as it begins to bloom.
source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Borage 50-60 d; direct-sow, taproot, thin to 12 in; self-sows); UMaine Bulletin #2076 (common borage among most-visited bee plants; self-seeding annual); Park Seed borage profile (classic companion claims: heavier strawberry fruiting, cucumber/squash yields, tomato hornworm note — garden lore).

name: Nasturtium
label: nasturtium edge

planting.note: 8 plants at 8-12 in (Johnny's); direct-sow 1/2-1 in deep after frost — roots resent transplant

bed30.note: two rows, or better: one row along the bed's edge so trailing types spill onto the path

watch_for: APHIDS — they swarm nasturtium by design (that's the trap crop working; Wisconsin/Penn State); flea beetles; cabbageworms; rich soil grows leaves with few flowers (Johnny's), so feed it nothing
watering: Well-drained, not rich, not wet; once the black aphids arrive, rinse them off or let them feed the hoverflies.
method_notes: Warm-season ANNUAL, frost-tender — the last flower out and the first to die. Its job in the Coleman-style bed is trap cropping: nasturtium's mustard-oil chemistry pulls aphids and cabbageworms off the brassicas and beans (Wisconsin Horticulture; Penn State's companion-planting piece) — but a trap crop only works as a monitored bait, so shake off or pinch out the aphid colonies before they explode and spill back. Everything — leaves, flowers, seed pods — is edible, but that is a harvest note, not a processing claim.
source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Nasturtium 55-65 d; direct-sow 1/2-1 in; 8-12 in spacing; low-fertility soil for blooms); Wisconsin Horticulture Extension nasturtium profile & Penn State Extension 'Herbs Make Good Plant Partners' (trap-crop mechanism); Burpee companion chart (nasturtium deters bean beetles).

name: Echinacea
label: echinacea corner

planting.note: 6 plants at 12-18 in; sow 8-10 wk inside or direct-sow in fall for natural stratification (Johnny's)

bed30.note: two rows at 12-18 in; give it the sunniest corner — it is a 3-4 ft statement plant

watch_for: ASTER YELLOWS — vectored by the aster leafhopper; UMaine's IPM page lists coneflowers among its hosts and UMaine's own Echinacea trials screened plants against it (leafhopper exclusion); Japanese beetles chew petals in July; powdery mildew
watering: Average, well-drained soil (Johnny's); drought-tolerant once established; water in the first summer only.
method_notes: RELIABLY HARDIY perennial (Johnny's: zones 3-10). The 300-365 day figure is Johnny's days-from-seeding to first bloom — a plant that flowers in year two and lives for years, so in the planner it is an establishment crop: it needs ~90 frost-free days to get going, then it overwinters. UMaine's bee-pasture work for wild blueberry pollination included echinacea in its flower mixes, and UMaine research on organic Echinacea production is the local fact base for it. Plant it as the pollinator anchor of the perennial corner; it is a garden plant here, not a medicinal crop.
source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (E. purpurea 300-365 d from seeding; zones 3-10; 8-10 wk indoor start; fall direct-sow option; powwow-type hybrids 126-165 d); UMaine IPM aster leafhopper factsheet (coneflowers as aster-yellows hosts); UMaine Echinacea organic-production trials (aster yellows worse in open field — screened cages); UMaine bee-pasture fact sheet for lowbush blueberry (echinacea in seed mixes).

name: Yarrow
label: yarrow edge

planting.note: 6 plants at 12-24 in (Johnny's); sow 8-10 wk inside, direct-sow late spring/fall; divide every 3-4 yr

bed30.note: two rows at 12 in; flat flower heads are landing pads for hoverflies and parasitic wasps — keep it at the bed corners

watch_for: powdery mildew in still, humid corners; aphids on stems; otherwise one of the toughest plants in the garden (zones 2-9, Johnny's: 'any well-drained soil')
watering: None once established — Johnny's calls it 'any well-drained soil' and it laughs at drought.
method_notes: RELIABLY HARDIY perennial (zones 2-9). This is the bed's insectary backbone: UConn's IPM lab insectary list documents common yarrow as a documented nectar and overwintering resource for hoverflies and parasitoid wasps — the same hoverflies whose larvae eat aphids (UMaine MHGN June 2025), and parasitoids that target brassica caterpillars and aphids. It blooms in the 120-130 day range from seed (Johnny's) and flowers all summer if cut; divide every 3-4 years to keep it vigorous (Johnny's).
source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Yarrow 120-130 d; zones 2-9; 8-10 wk indoor start; divide every 3-4 yr); UConn IPM & Entomology Lab insectary-plants list (Achillea millefolium: nectar/overwintering for hoverflies, parasitoids); Fedco (yarrow: perennial zones 3-10, full sun, good drainage, rebloom if cut back); UMaine MHGN June 2025 (hoverfly biology/aphid predation).

name: Bee balm
label: bee-balm corner

planting.note: 4 plants at 12-18 in (Johnny's), stretched toward 24 in where mildew pressure is high (Iowa State)

bed30.note: two rows at 18 in — and Iowa State says 2-2.5 ft apart, full sun, divided every 2-3 yr, or powdery mildew owns it by August

watch_for: POWDERY MILDEW — the defining complaint of the genus (Iowa State: worst on crowded plants and part shade; pick resistant cvs like Jacob Cline, Marshall's Delight, Raspberry Wine); rust in wet seasons
watering: Evenly moist soil likes it (it's a streambank plant), but water the soil, never overhead.
method_notes: RELIABLY HARDIY perennial (Johnny's: zones 4-10). From seed it 'does not usually flower until the second year' (Johnny's) — divisions flower the first year, so buy or split. This is the hummingbird and bee magnet of the perennial corner — UMaine's bee research names common beebalm among the red flowers with UV markings that bees read as more than red (Bulletin #2076) — making it real pollination support for the squash and cucumber rows. One rule governs where it goes: full sun, wide spacing, and division every 2-3 years, or mildew takes it.
source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Monarda: 6-8 wk indoor start; 12-18 in spacing; zones 4-10; flowers second year; divide mature plants); Iowa State University Extension (bee balm powdery mildew: full sun, space 2-2.5 ft, divide every 2-3 yr, resistant cultivars); UMaine Bulletin #2076 (common beebalm, red flowers with UV markings).
